NEUROAI · A VISUAL STORY

Learning beyond backpropagation

How a brain-plausible learning rule — predictive coding trained by prospective configuration — reaches the accuracy of error backpropagation while using only local updates. Told as a story on MNIST, from the conventional approach, through biological alternatives, to the comparison that explains why it works.

RESEARCH SUMMARY · ~4 PAGES
Inferring neural activity before plasticity — Song et al. (2024)

A detailed plain-language walkthrough of the Nature Neuroscience paper (Song, Millidge, Salvatori, Lukasiewicz, Xu & Bogacz, vol. 27, 348–358) introducing prospective configuration. Diagrams are our own schematic recreations of the paper's concepts; see the original article for Figures 1–4.

1MOTIVATION

Learning in the brain vs. backpropagation

IN PLAIN TERMS

Neural networks learn by adjusting connection strengths (weights) from their mistakes. The dominant method, backpropagation, computes a prediction, measures the error at the output, and propagates that error backwards to tell each weight how to change. It is the engine of modern AI — but as a model of the brain it is widely seen as implausible.

DETAIL

Three specific problems: (1) it needs a distinct backward pass with machinery separate from the forward pass; (2) that pass reuses the transpose of the forward weights (the “weight-transport problem”) — neurons have no obvious way to access their downstream weights in reverse; (3) it relies on a global error signal rather than the local signals a synapse actually sees. Backprop also causes interference: correcting one output can unintentionally worsen another the network already had right (the paper's water/salmon example).

WHY IT MATTERSThese issues motivate the search for a rule that is local and biologically realistic yet learns at least as well as backpropagation. The paper's answer is prospective configuration, realised in predictive coding networks.
Our recreation of the paper's Fig. 1 idea — interference under backprop vs. prospective configuration.
2THE PRINCIPLE

Prospective configuration: activity before plasticity

IN PLAIN TERMS

The central principle reverses the usual order of learning. Backprop changes weights first and lets activity follow. Prospective configuration instead first lets the network's neural activity settle into the state it would take after successful learning — a “prospective” configuration that already predicts the correct answer — and only then changes weights to make that state permanent.

DETAIL

The paper builds intuition with an energy machine: an energy-based network behaves like a physical system (nodes on posts connected by springs) that relaxes to its minimum-energy configuration. Clamping the input to the data and the output to the target, the system relaxes; the relaxed activity is the prospective state; the weights then move to lower the energy further. Because the network settles on a globally consistent state before any weight moves, the subsequent weight changes across layers reinforce rather than fight each other.

WHY IT MATTERSThis “look before you leap” is the source of every downstream advantage: less interference, faster convergence, and updates that stay aimed at the target even in deep networks.
Our recreation of the paper's Fig. 2 idea — relax to minimum energy first, then update weights.
3THE MODEL

Predictive coding networks & the equations

IN PLAIN TERMS

The paper instantiates the principle with predictive coding networks. Each layer has value neurons (current activity xₗ) and prediction-error neurons (εₗ), the mismatch between a layer's activity and the prediction made from the layer below. The network's energy is the total squared error.

DETAIL

Learning is a two-timescale process. Inference (relaxation): with input and output clamped, hidden value neurons repeatedly step downhill in energy — this is the neural dynamics. Weight update: once activity has settled, each weight takes one downhill step in the same energy, which turns out to be a simple product of a post-synaptic error and a pre-synaptic activity (Hebbian-like). Both use only signals available at adjacent neurons, so the whole scheme is local. The paper's Algorithm 1 uses γ = 0.1 and about 128 relaxation steps with an adaptive step size. Crucially, when the network can drive the energy to zero it provably minimises the loss too — so PC can match backprop.

KEY EQUATIONS
Energy   E = Σₗ ½‖εₗ‖²,  εₗ = xₗ − Wₗ₋₁ f(xₗ₋₁)  (Eqs. 6, 11)
Infer    Δxₗ = −γ ∂E/∂xₗ = −γ(εₗ − f′(xₗ)∘Wₗᵀ εₗ₊₁)  (Eq. 12)
Learn    ΔWₗ = α · εₗ₊₁ · f(xₗ)ᵀ  (Eq. 13)
WHY IT MATTERSOne quantity — prediction error — drives both “thinking” (relaxation) and “learning” (weight change), and both are local. That is precisely what makes the mechanism biologically credible, and it generalises to convolutional and other architectures via automatic differentiation of a per-layer forward function.
Our recreation of the paper's Fig. 2c — value neurons (blue) and error neurons (red).
4WHY IT DIFFERS

Target alignment: aiming the update at the goal

IN PLAIN TERMS

Backprop reduces the loss by adjusting each weight independently — but adjusting all weights at once can push the output in a direction that is not straight toward the target, because the layers' changes interfere. Prospective configuration, by first finding a target-consistent activity pattern, produces weight changes whose net effect on the output points much more directly at the desired answer.

DETAIL

The paper measures this with target alignment — the cosine of the angle between the direction the output actually moves during learning and the direction toward the target. Higher alignment means less wasted, interfering motion. Prospective configuration shows consistently higher target alignment than backprop, and — importantly — this is largely insensitive to the learning rate.

WHY IT MATTERSHigh target alignment is the quantitative fingerprint of “less interference”, and it directly predicts the practical advantages measured later (faster, more stable, less forgetting).
Our recreation of the paper's Fig. 3 idea — PC's update direction is better aligned with the target.
5DEPTH

The advantage grows with network depth

IN PLAIN TERMS

For a network with no hidden layers, backprop and prospective configuration behave identically. As layers are added, however, they diverge: backprop's target alignment falls with depth because weight changes in one layer interfere with those in others, whereas prospective configuration's alignment stays high.

DETAIL

The paper demonstrates this across randomly generated networks of increasing depth, holding everything else fixed. The gap widens monotonically with depth — exactly the regime where modern deep networks operate and where a biologically plausible advantage would matter most.

WHY IT MATTERSDepth is where the mechanism earns its keep: the deeper (and more brain-like) the network, the larger prospective configuration's edge over backpropagation.
Illustrative trend after the paper's Fig. 3e,h — alignment vs depth.
6EVIDENCE

Results across biologically relevant tasks

IN PLAIN TERMS

Beyond toy problems, the paper evaluates prospective configuration on a broad, realistic battery of tasks and finds it matches or beats backpropagation — with the largest gains in exactly the settings that matter for brains and real deployments.

DETAIL

Supervised image classification on FashionMNIST (fully-connected) and CIFAR-10 (convolutional); varying batch sizes down to fully online (batch = 1); continual learning across sequential tasks; concept/label drift; limited training data; and reinforcement-learning control (Acrobot, MountainCar, CartPole). Each compares an identical network trained either conventionally (backprop) or with prospective configuration, isolating the learning rule.

WHY IT MATTERSThe breadth is the paper's strongest empirical claim: not a narrow trick, but a general principle that is advantageous across the situations where learning is hardest — sequential, online, data-scarce and interactive.
Image classificationMatches or beats backprop on FashionMNIST (MLP) and CIFAR-10 (convolutional networks).
Continual learningLearns sequential tasks with far less catastrophic forgetting of earlier ones.
Concept / label driftAdapts faster when the meaning of classes changes mid-training.
Fewer examplesMore sample-efficient — higher accuracy from smaller training sets.
Online / small batchesRobust down to batch size 1, where backprop's advantage erodes.
Reinforcement learningFaster, more stable Q-learning on Acrobot, MountainCar and CartPole.
The paper's reported advantages (Fig. 4), summarised.
7PLAUSIBILITY

Biological grounding and significance

IN PLAIN TERMS

Because inference and learning both rely only on local prediction errors, predictive coding maps naturally onto cortical circuitry — value and error neurons, local recurrent connectivity, and Hebbian synaptic change. The paper argues prospective configuration also reproduces qualitative patterns seen in real neural activity and behaviour, and connects to a family of related energy-based models (e.g. GeneRec, target propagation, Almeida–Pineda), for which the same principle holds.

DETAIL

The main practical cost is that relaxation requires iterating the neural dynamics before each weight update, so a step is computationally heavier than a single backprop pass; the paper treats this as the price of biological realism and shows the accuracy/efficiency trade-off is favourable on the tasks studied.

WHY IT MATTERSThe significance: a single, local, energy-based principle that is both a plausible account of how brains might learn and a competitive — often superior — machine-learning algorithm. That is the meaning of the title, “learning beyond backpropagation.”
Our recreation of the paper's core loop — clamp, infer, learn.
OUR WORK
Implementation & results on MNIST

We implemented predictive coding (prospective configuration) inside a small network and ran it head-to-head against backpropagation and Hebbian learning. Every chart is from our own live experiments.

0THE SETUP

One task, one network, three ways to learn

WHAT YOU'RE SEEING

Ten handwritten-digit classes from MNIST, and a deliberately simple network: a single hidden layer (784 → 100 → C, sigmoid). Everything below uses this same architecture and the same training loop.

HOW IT'S DONE

We only ever change one thing between experiments — the rule that decides how weights are updated from a mistake. That isolation is what makes the comparison fair.

TAKEAWAYHold the model and data fixed; vary only the learning rule. Any difference we see is the rule, nothing else.
Sample MNIST validation digits.
↓We start with the rule that dominates modern AI — and ask whether a brain could actually run it.
1CONVENTIONAL

Backpropagation — the powerful, implausible baseline

WHAT YOU'RE SEEING

The reference model, trained on a 3-class subset. It learns quickly and cleanly to ~98% — this is the bar the biological rules must reach.

HOW IT'S DONE

A forward pass produces a prediction; the error is then sent backwards through the network, layer by layer, to assign blame to every weight (the chain rule).

ALGORITHM / METHOD
Δw = −α ∂ℒ/∂w  (global error, propagated backward)
TAKEAWAYBackprop works — but it needs a separate backward pass that reuses the transpose of the forward weights and a non-local error signal. Brains have no obvious way to do this. That is our motivation to look elsewhere.
Backpropagation on 3-class MNIST — loss and accuracy.
98.1%
backprop 3-class accuracy
↓If the brain can't send errors backward, can neurons learn from what's available locally? The classic idea: Hebbian learning.
2TOWARD BIOLOGY

Hebbian learning — local, but blind to the goal

WHAT YOU'RE SEEING

The first biologically plausible attempt: “neurons that fire together, wire together.” Each weight changes using only the activity of the two neurons it connects. On the 2-class panel (next step) Hebbian barely moves off chance; on 3 classes it collapses to ~36.1%.

HOW IT'S DONE

The update is a simple product of pre- and post-synaptic activity — no error is routed to the hidden layer, so the hidden weights get no signal about whether the answer was right.

ALGORITHM / METHOD
Δw ∝ (post-synaptic activity) · (pre-synaptic activity)
TAKEAWAYHebbian learning is local and plausible, but carries no target information into the hidden layer — so it can't reliably solve even easy tasks. Locality alone is not enough; we need locality and a goal signal.
3-class task — Hebbian (orange) sits at chance while backprop (blue) learns. Predictive coding (green) is previewed here.
↓Predictive coding keeps the locality of Hebbian learning — but adds a way to feel the goal, by inferring activity before changing any weight.
3THE IDEA

Predictive coding & prospective configuration

WHAT YOU'RE SEEING

The central idea of the paper: infer neural activity before plasticity. With the answer (target) pinned at the output, the network first relaxes its internal activity to a configuration that already predicts the target — the “prospective” state — and only then consolidates it with local weight changes. The 2-class panel shows the make-or-break detail: clamp the output and it learns; leave it free and it fails.

HOW IT'S DONE

Each layer carries a value node and a prediction-error node. Inference (relaxation) lowers a local energy by settling the hidden activity; the weights then descend that same energy with a Hebbian-like product of a prediction error and a pre-synaptic activity.

ALGORITHM / METHOD
Energy   E = Σ ½‖ε‖²,  εl = xl − Wl-1f(xl-1)
Infer    Δx = −γ ∂E/∂x  (output clamped to target)
Learn    ΔWl = α · εl+1 · f(xl)ᵀ
TAKEAWAYClamping the target during relaxation is what makes learning prospective: the inferred errors point the weights toward the answer. Unclamped, errors vanish and nothing is learned — the same failure mode as Hebbian.
2-class task: predictive coding learns only with the output clamped, then matches backprop and beats Hebbian.

4THE HARD TEST

Does it hold on a harder task?

WHAT YOU'RE SEEING

Moving to 3 classes, predictive coding (green) rides almost exactly on top of backpropagation (blue) and reaches ~98.5%, while Hebbian stays at chance. The learned hidden-unit weights below show the network has organised structured, input-sensitive filters — not noise.

HOW IT'S DONE

Identical setup to the backprop baseline; only the learning rule differs. The hidden weights are read straight out of the trained network.

TAKEAWAYPredictive coding is not a 2-class fluke — it tracks backprop on the harder task and learns genuine hidden-layer features, the very thing Hebbian learning could not do.
Top: 3-class accuracy. Bottom: predictive-coding learned hidden-unit weight patterns.
↓Three rules, one picture — how do they actually stack up?

Backprop vs Hebbian vs Predictive Coding

WHAT YOU'RE SEEING

Side by side across both tasks: predictive coding equals backpropagation and decisively beats Hebbian learning — while using only local, biologically plausible updates.

HOW IT'S DONE

Final validation accuracy after identical training budgets, averaged over the run.

TAKEAWAYPredictive coding closes the gap to backpropagation that Hebbian learning never could — the headline result of the story.

↓Matching backprop's accuracy is one thing — but why does a local rule behave like a global one? Two diagnostics answer it.
6aWHY — VARIANCE

Consistent updates: gradient signal-to-noise

WHAT YOU'RE SEEING

How consistent are the per-example weight updates? Higher SNR means less noisy, more reliable learning. Predictive coding shows the highest SNR of the three, especially in the output layer.

HOW IT'S DONE

For each rule we compute per-example gradients on held-out data and measure the signal-to-noise ratio (|mean| / standard deviation) in each layer.

ALGORITHM / METHOD
SNR = |mean(gradient)| / std(gradient)
TAKEAWAYPredictive coding's local updates are not noisy heuristics — they are consistent across examples, a prerequisite for stable learning.
Per-example gradient SNR (bars = mean, dots = layers).
RuleLayer 1Layer 2
Backprop0.1240.108
Hebbian0.3420.059
Predictive Coding0.3510.536
6bWHY — BIAS

Pointing the right way: alignment with backprop

WHAT YOU'RE SEEING

Do the updates point in the same direction as backpropagation's true gradient? This “target alignment” is the paper's core explanation. Predictive coding is positively aligned in both layers; Hebbian carries little aligned signal, especially in the hidden layer.

HOW IT'S DONE

During training we periodically compute both the rule's gradient and backprop's gradient on the same data, and measure the cosine similarity between them, layer by layer.

ALGORITHM / METHOD
cos(θ) = (grule · gbackprop) / (‖grule‖ ‖gbackprop‖)
TAKEAWAYPredictive coding approximates the backprop gradient with local computation — the mechanism behind its backprop-level accuracy, and what Hebbian learning fundamentally lacks.
Cosine similarity of each rule's gradients to backprop's, across epochs.
7CONCLUSION

The story, in one arc

FROM CONVENTIONAL TO BIOLOGICAL — AND BACK TO PERFORMANCE
  • Backpropagation sets the accuracy bar (~98%) but is biologically implausible — it needs a global backward pass.
  • Hebbian learning is local and plausible, but blind to the goal in its hidden layer, so it stalls near chance.
  • Predictive coding keeps Hebbian-style locality yet, by inferring activity before plasticity with the target clamped, produces updates that align with backprop — reaching backprop-level accuracy.
  • Why it works: its gradients are both consistent (high SNR) and well-aligned with the true gradient (high target alignment) — a local rule that behaves like a global one.
  • The punchline: learning “beyond backpropagation” — matching its performance with a rule a brain could plausibly run.

③ RESEARCH PROJECT · FRESHGRAD CONTINUAL LEARNING
Learning Without Letting Go: Predictive Coding beyond Backpropagation in Continual Learning

Backpropagation modifies all weights from a single global error signal; the brain instead settles neural activity first, then makes local weight changes — which should be less prone to catastrophic interference. We test whether predictive coding (PC, prospective configuration) is more robust than backprop (BP) for online / continual learning, on the same architecture. Three questions, answered below with live experiments.

Permuted-MNIST (10) · Split-MNIST (5)

Protocol: PC uses the Song-2024 relaxation (output clamped to the one-hot target, hidden nodes relaxed, local Hebbian weight update — Eqs. 12–13). Results are single-seed, single-pass, shallow-net proofs-of-concept; trends are what matter, not decimal points.

Q1STATIC PARITY

Same network, two learning rules

THE QUESTION

On static MNIST, how do PC and BP compare on the same network — train error, test error, and the consistency (covariance / SNR) of their per-example gradients?

RESULT

Near-parity in accuracy: BP reaches 5.8% test error, PC 6.6% (5 epochs). But PC’s per-example gradients are far more consistent — higher signal-to-noise, especially in the deeper layer.

WHY IT MATTERSPC is a viable BP alternative on the base task, and its lower-variance updates hint at why it may transfer better across tasks — the credit-assignment signal is less noisy.
Left: train/test error — PC within ~1pt of BP. Right: per-example gradient SNR (higher = more consistent updates); PC exceeds BP in both layers.
Q2CONTINUAL METRICS

Online accuracy, transfer & forgetting

THE PROTOCOL

A fixed single-pass continual stream. After each task we fill the accuracy matrix R[i,j] (test acc on task j after training through task i) and read off the standard metrics.

ACC     = mean_j R[N,j]
BWT    = mean_(j<N) ( R[N,j] − R[j,j] )
Forget = mean_j ( max_i R[i,j] − R[N,j] )
RESULT

On Permuted-MNIST PC forgets far less (BWT -3.0 vs -7.1; forgetting 3.6% vs 8.4%) but trails on raw final accuracy (55.4% vs 63.3%). On Split-MNIST PC wins on both: 71.2% vs 67.0% accuracy and less forgetting.

THE TRADEOFFPC buys stability (retention) at some cost to plasticity (raw accuracy) under permutation; when tasks share structure (Split), it is simply better.
GEM/Chaudhry metrics, BP vs PC. Lower |BWT| and Forgetting = more robust; higher Final Acc = more capable.
Q2PLASTICITY

BP’s representations collapse; PC’s don’t

LOSS OF PLASTICITY

Dohare et al. (Nature 2024) show BP networks progressively lose the ability to learn over a task sequence — visible as a collapse in the effective rank (participation ratio) of their hidden representations.

RESULT

BP’s effective rank falls monotonically (15→8 over 10 tasks) — representation collapse. PC holds steady near 30, roughly 2× higher, showing no plasticity loss.

WHY IT MATTERSThis is the clearest signal in the study: PC’s local, activity-driven updates preserve representational capacity where BP erodes it — the mechanistic basis for less forgetting. (Dead-unit fraction stayed 0% for both at this depth, so effective rank is the informative signature.)
Effective rank of hidden activations vs tasks seen. BP (blue) collapses; PC (orange) is stable — no loss of plasticity.
Q2ADAPTATION

Speed vs retention, made visible

ADAPTATION SPEED

Within the first new permuted task, BP’s batch accuracy climbs faster than PC’s — BP adapts quicker in-the-moment. Per-task online accuracy stays higher for BP too.

RETENTION MAP

The R matrices make the tradeoff visual: BP’s earlier-task columns dim more as training proceeds (forgetting); PC’s stay brighter.

THE OTHER SIDEBP is the faster, higher-accuracy learner moment-to-moment; PC’s advantage is purely in holding on to what it learned.
Left: accuracy climb on the first permuted task (adaptation speed). Right: online accuracy per task.
Accuracy matrices R[i,j]: rows = after training task i, columns = task evaluated. Brighter lower-left in PC = better retention.
Q3INFERENCE BUDGET

More relaxation ≠ better here

THE QUESTION

PC’s inner relaxation runs T steps before each weight update. Does a bigger inference budget buy a better stability–plasticity balance — and what does it cost?

RESULT

Across T = 1…32, final accuracy (56→53%) and forgetting stay essentially flat, while wall-clock grows ~linearly in T. Even T=1 learns well — consistent with Rosenbaum’s result that one-step PC approximates backprop.

WHY IT MATTERSFor a shallow MLP, spending more inference is wasted compute: small T is on the compute–accuracy Pareto front. Budget likely matters more for deeper nets — a clear next experiment.
Left: accuracy & forgetting vs relaxation steps T (log scale), BP accuracy as dashed reference. Right: wall-clock vs T — roughly linear.
ANSWER TO THE HYPOTHESIS

Does local, activity-first learning resist forgetting? Largely yes.

  • Q1 — parity. PC matches BP on static MNIST (6.6% vs 5.8% test error) with markedly more consistent gradients.
  • Q2 — robustness. PC roughly halves forgetting on Permuted-MNIST and preserves effective rank where BP’s collapses; on Split-MNIST it beats BP on accuracy and retention. The cost is lower raw plasticity (slower adaptation, lower peak accuracy) under permutation.
  • Q3 — cheap inference suffices. Stability–plasticity is flat in T for this net while cost is linear; small T wins. Depth is the variable to probe next.
  • Takeaway. The brain-plausible objection to backprop has teeth: activity-first, local updates trade a little plasticity for real robustness — exactly the regime continual learning cares about.
CAVEATS

Single seed, single-pass, one hidden layer, MNIST subsets. Directional evidence, not final numbers. Grounding: Song et al. 2024 (mechanism), Dohare et al. 2024 (plasticity metric), Lopez-Paz & Ranzato 2017 (BWT/forgetting), Rosenbaum 2022 (T=1 ≈ backprop).

① SUMMARY OF THE PAPER — ROSENBAUM (2022)
On the relationship between predictive coding and backpropagation

A plain-language walkthrough of the PLOS ONE paper (17(3):e0266102; arXiv:2106.13082) that pins down exactly when predictive coding computes the same gradients as backpropagation — and when it does not. Diagrams are our own schematic recreations of the paper's ideas; it also ships Torch2PC, a library that runs PC on any PyTorch nn.Sequential.

R1THE QUESTION

How can a local, iterative rule relate to backprop?

IN PLAIN TERMS

Backpropagation is the workhorse of deep learning, but it is biologically awkward: it needs a separate backward pass that reuses the transpose of the forward weights and ships a precise, non-local error signal back through the network. Predictive coding is the opposite — a network of neurons that only ever talk to their neighbours, settling their activity by local message-passing. People had claimed the two are “equivalent.”

THE PRECISE ASK

Rosenbaum makes the claim exact: under what conditions does a PC network's weight update equal the backprop gradient, and where does the equivalence quietly break?

WHY IT MATTERSIf PC only equals backprop under special assumptions, then results attributed to “using PC” may really be results of backprop in disguise — a distinction this paper makes measurable.
Backprop needs a biologically impossible backward pathway; predictive coding uses only local messages between neighbouring neurons.
R2THE SET-UP

Value nodes, error nodes, an inner loop

HOW IT WORKS

Each layer of a feedforward net is given two extra quantities: a value/belief node vₗ that holds the layer's current activity, and a prediction-error node εₗ that measures the mismatch between a layer's activity and what the layer above predicts for it. Learning has an inner loop (relax the beliefs) wrapped by an outer step (update the weights) — unlike backprop's single backward sweep.

STRICT (BIOLOGICAL) PC

In the strict form the predictions keep moving as the beliefs relax, so the errors chase a moving target.

εₗ = fₗ(vₗ₋₁) − vₗ
vₗ ← vₗ + η(εₗ − εₗ₊₁·∂f/∂v)
THE NUANCEStrict PC genuinely learns the task — but its weight updates do not equal the backprop gradient. Good training is not the same as correct gradients.
PC's two phases: first settle the activity (an inner loop repeated n times), then make one local weight update.
R3THE KEY IDEA

The Fixed Prediction Assumption (FPA)

IN PLAIN TERMS

The pivotal move: freeze the predictions at the values they took on the forward pass (call them v̂ₗ), and pin the top error node to the true loss gradient. This linearises the inner loop around the forward pass — the beliefs now relax through a simple, fixed set of connections.

HOW IT WORKS

With predictions frozen, each error node relaxes toward the error signal handed down from above through the forward Jacobian — one layer deeper per iteration.

εₗ = v̂ₗ − vₗ,   εₖ = ∂ℒ/∂v̂ₖ (clamped)
vₗ ← vₗ + η(εₗ − Jₗ₊₁ᵀεₗ₊₁)
WHY IT MATTERSAt the fixed point the error nodes become exactly the backprop error signals, ε*ₗ = ∂ℒ/∂v̂ₗ — so the local, Hebbian-looking weight update equals the global backprop gradient.
Our schematic: predictions are frozen at the forward values; the error nodes then relax to the backprop signal.
R4THREE MODES

Exact, or a tunable dial toward backprop

THE RESULT

This gives three regimes. Exact solves the fixed point in closed form and equals backprop to machine precision. FixedPred reaches it iteratively — with step size η=1 and iterations n≥depth it recovers backprop exactly; with fewer/softer steps it is a controllable approximation. Strict never equals backprop.

THE DIAL

So the number of inference iterations n and the step size η are literally a knob between “roughly right” and “exactly backprop.”

THE COSTThe inner relaxation makes iterative PC many× slower than one backprop pass — the paper reports order-of-magnitude slowdowns on CIFAR-scale nets.
The three Torch2PC modes as a dial: Strict → FixedPred → Exact, converging onto backprop.
R5THE BOTTOM LINE

“PC = backprop” is real — but conditional

WHY IT MATTERS

The popular equivalence holds only under the FPA and a converged inner loop; the biologically faithful (strict) PC does not equal backprop. The paper turns a loose slogan into a precise, testable statement — and gives the tooling (Torch2PC, modes) to check it.

THE TAKEAWAY FOR THIS STUDYAny advantage credited to “PC” must say which regime — because in the FPA regime PC simply is backprop. Our Research tab tests exactly this.
ModeErrorIterates?Relation to backprop

The FreshGrad questions Q1 / Q2 / Q3, answered with this paper's PC

The same three research questions as the Song section — static parity, continual robustness, inference budget — now with PC = Fixed-Prediction PC (FPA). This makes the three papers directly comparable on identical protocols.

Q1STATIC PARITY

Same task, does PC match backprop?

RESULT

Under the FPA, PC computes backprop's gradient, so it matches backprop almost exactly. Test error PC 4.3% vs backprop 4.3%.

READOn the base task the two are on par; the interesting differences are continual (Q2).
Q1 — train/test error and per-example gradient SNR, PC vs backprop.
Q2CONTINUAL ROBUSTNESS

Online accuracy, forgetting, backward transfer, plasticity

RESULT

Backprop and FPA-PC are indistinguishable on Permuted-MNIST (accuracy 64% vs 64%, forgetting 10% vs 10%) — including the same loss of plasticity. PC inherits backprop's continual behaviour exactly.

BWT = mean⃺<ₙ(R[N,j]−R[j,j])  Forget = mean⃺(maxₕ R[i,j]−R[N,j])

Q3INFERENCE BUDGET

Does more relaxation buy robustness?

RESULT

Accuracy and forgetting are flat across T: at η=1 the FPA recovers the backprop gradient at any inference budget, so more relaxation changes nothing (but still costs compute).

READStability–plasticity vs the number of relaxation steps T, against a linear compute cost.
Accuracy & forgetting vs inference steps T (left); wall-clock vs T (right).
TAKEAWAY

Under the FPA, PC just is backprop — including its forgetting.

  • FPA-PC matches backprop on static accuracy, continual accuracy, forgetting AND effective-rank collapse.
  • So the robustness reported in the Song section comes from the strict / prospective regime, not from “using PC” per se.
  • Rosenbaum's contribution is exactly this clarification: PC = backprop only under the FPA.

Single-seed, single-pass, shallow-net proofs-of-concept; directional evidence. Grounding: Rosenbaum 2022 (arXiv:2106.13082).

① SUMMARY OF THE PAPER — BOGACZ (2017)
A tutorial on the free-energy framework for modelling perception and learning

A plain-language walkthrough of the Journal of Mathematical Psychology tutorial (76:198–211) — the canonical, step-by-step derivation of predictive coding from the free-energy principle. Diagrams are our own schematic recreations of the paper's circuits. Its signature idea is precision-weighting: every error is divided by its own (learned) variance.

B1THE PROBLEM

Infer a hidden cause from noisy sensation

IN PLAIN TERMS

An organism sees a noisy signal u (say, a light intensity) and must infer the hidden cause φ behind it (say, the size of a food item). It assumes a Gaussian prior on φ and a Gaussian likelihood of u given φ. The exact Bayesian answer needs an intractable normalising integral.

HOW IT WORKS

The framework represents the guess φ, the top-down prediction g(φ), and the mismatch between prediction and observation as activities of distinct neurons wired to their neighbours.

THE MOVERather than compute the exact posterior, the brain maximises a tractable objective — the (negative variational) free energy F — using only local messages.
Our schematic of the generative model: hidden cause φ predicts sensation u; an error node carries the mismatch.
B2THE OBJECTIVE

Free energy F, and why maximising it works

HOW IT WORKS

F is the log-joint probability evaluated at the current guess. Bogacz shows (§3) that maximising F is equivalent to minimising the KL divergence between an approximate posterior and the true one — so a system that climbs F is doing approximate Bayesian inference.

F = ln p(φ) + ln p(u|φ)
= ½[ −(φ−vₚ)²/Σₚ − (u−g(φ))²/Σᵘ − lnΣₚ − lnΣᵘ ] + C
WHY IT MATTERSOne scalar F ties together perception (inferring φ), learning (the weights), and precision — all as gradient ascent on the same quantity.
Maximising free energy F finds the guess where the prior belief and the sensory evidence best agree.
B3PRECISION-WEIGHTED ERRORS

Every error divided by its variance

IN PLAIN TERMS

The gradient of F is carried by two prediction-error terms — a prior error and a sensory error. Each is a raw mismatch scaled by precision (inverse variance): reliable channels shout, noisy channels whisper.

εₚ = (φ − vₚ) / Σₚ  (prior)
εᵘ = (u − g(φ)) / Σᵘ  (sensory)
THE DIFFERENCE vs SONGSong's supervised PCN uses unit precision (Σ=I) — plain squared error. Bogacz's distinctive ingredient is learnable precision, which is what our Research tab shows paying off on unreliable inputs.
Precision as a reliability weight: the same raw error counts for more from a low-variance (reliable) channel.
B4INFERENCE + LEARNING

One circuit, two timescales

HOW IT WORKS

On a fast timescale the value nodes relax by gradient ascent on F (perception). On a slow timescale, once activity has settled, the weights follow a purely local Hebbian rule — a product of a pre-synaptic activity and a post-synaptic error. Nothing needs a global signal or a transported weight.

φ̇ = εᵘ g′(φ) − εₚ  (infer, fast)
Δθ ∝ εᵘ h(φ)  (learn, slow · Hebbian)
WHY IT MATTERSThe exact same prediction-error signal drives both perception and learning, and both are local — the core reason the framework is biologically plausible.
Two timescales in one circuit: activity settles fast (perception), weights change slowly (learning).
B5LEARNABLE PRECISION

Variance is learned too — by an interneuron

IN PLAIN TERMS

Precision itself is learned by climbing F. The multivariate rule needs a matrix inverse — awkward for a neuron — so Bogacz adds an inhibitory interneuron that computes the raw error, making the precision update strictly local.

∂F/∂Σ = ½(ε² − Σ⁻¹) →  interneuron: ΔΣ = α(ε·e − 1) → Σ → Var
WHY IT MATTERSPrecision behaves like attention — the brain up-weights reliable evidence. One local circuit thus does perception, weight learning and precision learning, all from the same free-energy principle.
Our schematic of the interneuron circuit that learns each error node's variance without a matrix inverse.

③ RESEARCH PROJECT — BOGACZ
The FreshGrad questions Q1 / Q2 / Q3, answered with this paper's PC

The same three research questions as the Song section — static parity, continual robustness, inference budget — now with PC = precision-weighted PC. This makes the three papers directly comparable on identical protocols.

Q1STATIC PARITY

Same task, does PC match backprop?

RESULT

Precision-weighted PC matches backprop on static MNIST (both ~98%). Test error PC 2.3% vs backprop 2.4%.

Q2CONTINUAL ROBUSTNESS

Online accuracy, forgetting, backward transfer, plasticity

RESULT

On Permuted-MNIST the precision-weighted PC actually forgets more than backprop (forgetting 29% vs 13%; accuracy 58% vs 71%) — hidden-layer precision does not, by itself, protect earlier tasks.

BWT = mean⃺<ₙ(R[N,j]−R[j,j])  Forget = mean⃺(maxₕ R[i,j]−R[N,j])

Q3INFERENCE BUDGET

Does more relaxation buy robustness?

RESULT

More relaxation (larger T) gives modest, monotone gains in continual accuracy — the inference budget helps a little, at a roughly linear compute cost.

READStability–plasticity vs the number of relaxation steps T, against a linear compute cost.
Accuracy & forgetting vs inference steps T (left); wall-clock vs T (right).
TAKEAWAY

Precision is the mechanism — it shines on reliability, not automatically on forgetting.

  • On static MNIST precision-weighted PC matches backprop with more consistent gradients.
  • Its distinctive win is heteroscedastic inference (cue-combination, Paper Summary), where learned precision approaches the optimal estimator.
  • On plain continual MNIST, precision on the hidden layer does not curb forgetting — a clean, honest negative result.

Single-seed, single-pass, shallow-net proofs-of-concept; directional evidence. Grounding: Bogacz 2017 (J. Math. Psychol. 76:198–211).

④ CROSS-PAPER COMPARISON
The same idea, three relationships to backprop

Three formulations of predictive coding — Song's prospective configuration, Rosenbaum's fixed-prediction PC, Bogacz's precision-weighted PC — answered the same research questions (Q1–Q3). Here we place them side by side. Because each was trained in its own regime, we compare each PC against its own matched backprop baseline (a relationship, not an absolute score): does PC forget less, the same, or more than backprop?

C1THE VERDICT

One idea, three outcomes

THE RESULT

On Permuted-MNIST, relative to its own backprop baseline: Song's PC forgets ~2× less (3.6% vs 8.4%), Rosenbaum's PC is identical to backprop (9.9% vs 9.9%), and Bogacz's PC forgets more (29.1% vs 12.6%).

WHY THEY DIFFERRosenbaum's FPA-PC is backprop, so it forgets identically. Song's activity-first relaxation reduces interference — genuinely beyond backprop. Bogacz's precision helps reliability, not this kind of forgetting.
PC forgetting ÷ backprop forgetting — below 1 is more robust, above 1 less.
C2THE DETAILS

Forgetting and preserved capacity

WHAT YOU'RE SEEING

Left: each PC's forgetting against its own backprop. Right: the effective rank left in the hidden representation after 10 tasks — a proxy for how much capacity to keep learning survives (loss of plasticity).

NUANCEBoth Song and Bogacz keep higher effective rank than backprop; but only Song turns that into less forgetting. High rank alone doesn't guarantee retention.
Permuted-MNIST forgetting, PC vs its own backprop.
Effective rank retained after 10 tasks.
C3THE COMMON GROUND

All three match backprop on the base task

Q1 PARITY

Whatever their continual-learning behaviour, all three predictive-coding variants reach backprop-level accuracy on static MNIST — so the differences above are about robustness, not raw capability.

READPredictive coding is a viable learning rule in every formulation; the papers differ on what it buys you beyond that.
Static-MNIST test error, PC vs backprop, per paper.
SUMMARY
PaperPC formulationForgetting vs BPEffective rankVerdict
Songprospective configuration~2× lesspreserved (high)beyond backprop
Rosenbaumfixed-prediction (FPA)identicalidentical to BP= backprop (by construction)
Bogaczprecision-weightedmorehigh, but forgetswins on reliability, not forgetting
TAKEAWAY

“Does predictive coding beat backprop?” depends entirely on which PC.

  • Song — activity settles before weights move: less interference, preserved plasticity, less forgetting. The genuine “beyond backprop” case.
  • Rosenbaum — under the fixed-prediction assumption PC computes backprop's gradient, so it inherits backprop's behaviour exactly.
  • Bogacz — precision-weighting is about reliability (heteroscedastic inference), and does not, by itself, reduce catastrophic forgetting.
  • The three papers aren't rivals — they're complementary views: Bogacz gives the mechanism, Song the training principle that exploits it, Rosenbaum the precise bridge back to backprop.

Cross-paper comparison uses each PC against its own matched backprop baseline (regimes differ, so absolutes aren't directly comparable). Single-seed, single-pass, shallow-net.

Research Project — team presentation deck

One slide per team member (use ← → arrow keys or the buttons). Built around the final research proposal.

① THE PROBLEM
1 / 9

Backpropagation — powerful, but not brain-like

  • Neural nets learn by backpropagation: predict, then send the output error backward through every layer to update the weights.
  • A brain can’t run it — it needs weight transport (the exact transpose weights, in reverse), a global non-local error, and a separate backward phase.
  • And it forgets: learning new tasks overwrites the old ones (catastrophic interference).
✗ × 3
things a brain can’t do
② THE IDEA
2 / 9

Predictive coding — learning with only local signals

  • PC gives each layer value neurons (its activity) and error neurons (local mismatch); it settles activity first, then makes a local Hebbian weight update.
  • That removes all three blockers — no global error, no weight transport, no separate backward pass: everything is local.
  • We test it on an identical MLP (swap only the rule) with three questions — Q1 parity · Q2 forgetting · Q3 budget.
100% local
only neighbour signals
Q1 · THE QUESTION
3 / 9

Does PC match backprop on the basics?

  • On plain static MNIST, is predictive coding as accurate as backprop on the same network?
  • Test error — % wrong on held-out data; the generalisation number that actually matters.
  • Gradient SNR — how consistent the per-example weight updates are; high = a clean, reliable learning signal.
same net
two rules · one test
Q1 · RESULTS
4 / 9

Predictive coding matches backprop

  • PC reaches backprop-level test error on static MNIST (~6%, either rule).
  • Its per-example gradients are more consistent — higher SNR, a cleaner signal than backprop’s.
  • So PC is a fully viable learning rule; its real advantage shows up in continual learning.
PC ≈ BP
static accuracy — on par
Q2 · THE QUESTION
5 / 9

Can it keep learning without forgetting?

  • Train on a stream of tasks (Permuted & Split MNIST), one pass each — does learning new tasks erase the old?
  • Forgetting / backward transfer — the drop in an earlier task’s accuracy after later training.
  • Loss of plasticity — whether the net keeps enough active, diverse hidden units to keep learning (effective rank).
task 10 → task 1
still remembered?
Q2 · RESULTS
6 / 9

PC forgets far less than backprop

  • On Permuted-MNIST, PC roughly halves forgetting vs backprop.
  • Backprop’s hidden representation collapses (effective rank falls); PC’s stays high and flat.
  • Preserved capacity is the mechanism behind the lower forgetting — the core beyond-backprop result.
3.6% vs 8.4%
forgetting: PC vs backprop
Q3 · THE QUESTION
7 / 9

How much “thinking” before it learns?

  • PC settles its activity for T steps before each weight update — how much T is actually worth it?
  • Inference budget T — the number of settling (relaxation) steps per batch.
  • Stability–plasticity vs compute — more T may buy robustness, but costs linearly more compute.
how long?
to think before learning
Q3 · RESULTS
8 / 9

A little thinking goes a long way

  • Accuracy and forgetting stay roughly flat across T = 1 … 32.
  • Compute cost grows ~linearly with T.
  • A small inference budget captures most of the benefit — long relaxation isn’t worth the cost.
small T wins
robustness flat · cost linear
THE VERDICT
9 / 9

Three views of predictive coding

  • Song settle then learn · Rosenbaum equals backprop under the FPA · Bogacz weight errors by reliability.
  • Forgetting vs backprop — Song 0.43× (better) · Rosenbaum 1.0× (same) · Bogacz 2.3× (worse).
  • Conclusion: activity-first PC (Song) beats backprop at continual learning. Next: deeper nets · more seeds · CIFAR.
